cover.headline: Margins and valuation are both at a low: the business is intact, the leadership premium is not
cover.lead: Maruti is India's default car brand. It sells 2 of every 5 cars in India, makes 49% of India's passenger-vehicle (PV) exports and holds ₹{{fin.treasury.11|num}} cr of cash with no debt. But it is no longer the near-monopoly of FY19, when it had a 51% share. It lost the SUV decade to M&M, Tata and Hyundai. Its Q1FY27 EBITDA margin (operating profit as % of sales) was 8.6% (standalone). That is the lowest in its listed history outside COVID. The stock has fallen {{P.returns.1y|chg}} in a year and trades at {{V.pe.current|x}} trailing earnings. That is the 2nd percentile of its 10-year range: cheaper than 98% of the past decade. We think the market is treating the margin low as permanent. We disagree, but we also do not expect the old valuation premium to return. **We initiate with BUY and a target price of {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): 25x Sep-28E EPS, the way the street values Maruti and its own five-year median.** Our DCF and EV/EBITDA cross-checks land within 5% of it.

arguments.h: GST 2.0 revived the one segment Maruti truly owns
arguments.p: In Sep-2025 the GST on small cars was cut from 28% plus cess to 18%. PV industry growth swung from −0.4% in H1FY26 to +16.7% in H2FY26 and +28% in H1FY27. Small cars are ~48% of Maruti's domestic volume, and Maruti holds most of that segment. So the benefit lands almost entirely on Maruti. Its market share recovered from 39.3% (FY26) to 41.0% (H1FY27).

arguments.h: The margin fall is mostly cyclical; only ~150bp is structural
arguments.p: Margins fell ~370bp (basis points; 100bp = 1 percentage point) quarter-on-quarter in Q1FY27. About 300bp came from commodities: aluminium, plastics and PGMs (precious metals used in catalytic converters), after the West Asia conflict. Of this, ~110bp was a one-off change in the timing of supplier settlements. Price hikes in June and August, plus that reversal, should lift margins back to ~11% by H2. Three things will not come back: the heavier small-car mix, higher depreciation on new plants and EV launch costs. We model EBITDA margins of {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}} for FY27-29E, versus 13%+ in FY24-25.

arguments.h: Competitive edge: strong in reach and trust, not in cost, SUVs or EVs
arguments.p: Maruti's moat (lasting competitive advantage) is its network: 4,601 sales outlets and 5,926 service points, ~3x Hyundai or Tata. It also has the best resale values in its segments and ~70% of factory-fitted CNG cars. It no longer has a margin advantage: its Q1FY27 EBIT margin was 5.1%, versus 7.1% for M&M's auto business (PBIT). It holds ~4% of India's EV market versus Tata's 39%, and ~20% of SUVs. So we value it as a cash-generating volume business, not a compounding monopoly.

arguments.h: The valuation already prices in a lot of bad news
arguments.p: The stock trades at {{V.pe.current|x}} trailing P/E (share price ÷ earnings per share), against a 10-year median of {{V.pe.windows.10y.median|x}}. Its EV/EBITDA (company value including debt and cash ÷ operating profit) is {{V.evEbitda.current|x}}. Net cash of ~{{fin.treasury.11|num}} cr is ~23% of its market value. Our bear case ({{scen.bear.tp|inr}}) implies {{scen.bear.upside|chg}}, against {{scen.bull.upside|chg}} in our bull case. Our FY27E EPS of {{F.eps.0|inr}} is ~5% below consensus ({{R.street.consensus.0.eps|inr}}). The stock works even on these lower numbers.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results on 27-Oct-2026: the first test of margin recovery (supplier settlement reversal plus price hikes).
Festive retail sales (Oct–Nov) and the ~130k order book: these will show whether GST demand was simply pulled forward.
New launches: a 3-row SUV and a second EV in CY27; e-Vitara exports to Europe and Japan.
Commodity prices: aluminium is off its June peak; any easing in West Asia would help.

sections.title: Is there a tailwind? Yes, but it has changed shape

blocks.p: India sold {{R.industry.industryVolumes.14.domesticPV|num}} passenger vehicles (PVs) in FY26. That is ~34 cars per 1,000 people, versus ~80-90 in Indonesia, ~220-250 in China and ~280 in Thailand. Low car ownership is the classic bull case, and it is real. But it has been 'about to happen' for 15 years. Domestic PV volumes grew only **~4.5% a year from FY14 to FY26**. FY19–FY22 was a lost half-decade. COVID, BS-VI emission norms, higher insurance costs and the chip shortage pushed the market back to FY16 levels.

exhibit.title: Domestic PV volumes: a decade of 4-5% growth, then a GST-driven jump
exhibit.unit: Domestic PV wholesale, i.e. factory dispatches to dealers (lakh units)

blocks.p: The bigger change is **what** India buys. Utility vehicles (UVs, mostly SUVs) rose from 21% of PV sales in FY16 to ~68% in FY26. Hatchbacks fell from ~46% at their FY19 peak to ~23%. This is the main reason Maruti's share fell from 51% to 39%. It was a hatchback company in an SUV market.

blocks.h: Three tailwinds for the next three years

bullets: **GST 2.0 (22-Sep-2025):** GST on small cars (up to 4m long, petrol engine up to 1.2L) fell from 28% plus cess (~29-31% in total) to 18%. That is a ~8-10% price cut on entry cars. First-time buyers rose from 42% to 51-54% of Maruti's sales. This is the first policy in a decade that favours the small car.

**Alternative fuels:** CNG (compressed natural gas), hybrids and EVs together crossed 40% of retail sales in Aug-2026 (petrol: 41%). CNG alone is ~25% of the market and ~40% of Maruti's volumes. Maruti built this segment and holds most of it.
**Exports:** India's PV exports rose from ~0.4mn (FY21) to ~0.9mn (FY26). India is becoming Suzuki's global hub for small cars and EVs (e-Vitara goes to Europe and Japan).

**Pull-forward risk:** H1FY27 grew +28% on a weak base, and some demand may have been brought forward. ICRA (+4-6%) and CRISIL (+5-7%) still forecast modest full-year growth. FY28 will be compared against a very high base.
**Rates and affordability:** RBI raised the repo rate to 5.50% on 7-Oct-2026. About 80% of cars are bought with a loan.

**Competition:** there are six credible SUV makers (M&M, Tata, Hyundai, Kia, Toyota, Maruti), plus new entrants (VinFast, BYD). Discounting is structurally higher than in the years when two companies dominated.

sections.title: How big can India get? Lessons from China and Toyota in Japan

blocks.p: India has ~38 cars per 1,000 people at ~US$9,400 GDP per capita (PPP, adjusted for local prices). Indonesia (~100) and China (~333) show where markets go as incomes cross US$10-15k. **China's car sales grew ~12x between 2002 and 2016** (1.1mn → 24.4mn) once incomes crossed this zone. India will not repeat China's boom, which was driven by credit and infrastructure. But even a third of that path would double India's market within a decade.

pair.title: Cars per 1,000 people vs income: India is at the start of the curve
pair.source: World Bank, OICA, national sources, GAM Research

pair.title: China car sales: the rapid growth phase India has not had yet

blocks.callout: **The lesson for market leaders:** in mature markets, the largest volume player keeps a lasting but lower share. Toyota has held ~30% of Japan's market for five decades. Hyundai-Kia held ~70-80% of Korea behind import barriers. India is neither protected nor brand-loyal. Our base case is that Maruti settles at **38-42% share of a much larger market**, not that it returns to 50%.

sections.title: Tailwind test: who captures the sector's growth?

blocks.p: A sector tailwind helps a shareholder only if the company captures it. We score each driver on whether Maruti is the main beneficiary, one of several beneficiaries, or a bystander.

verdicts: Maruti sells most of India's small cars under 4m. Mini and compact cars were 48% of its Q1FY27 domestic volume (mini +124% YoY).
The largest and most direct beneficiary. Its market share rose 2.3 percentage points YoY in Q1FY27.
Entry-level cars, CNG and 4,000+ outlets that reach tier-3/4 towns and rural areas (~45% of sales).
Rising car ownership flows through Maruti's showrooms more than anyone else's.
Shift to SUVs and premium cars
Brezza, Grand Vitara, Fronx and Victoris made Maruti #1 in SUVs by volume again. But it has only ~20-25% of the SUV segment, versus ~50% share overall.
It takes part but does not lead. M&M and Tata earn the SUV premium.
Maruti created the factory-fitted CNG market. About 40% of its volume is CNG.
A niche where Maruti has a cost advantage and rivals under-invested.
Grand Vitara and Victoris hybrids use Toyota technology. Policy support is uncertain (no GST relief).
Depends on CAFE-III credits (fuel-efficiency norms) and on pricing.
Its first EV (e-Vitara) arrived only in Aug-2025 and is mostly exported. Tata (~39%), M&M (~24%) and MG (~20%) lead India's EV market.
A late entrant. If EVs reach 15%+ of sales by 2030, faster than expected, Maruti could lose share.
~49% of India's PV exports in FY26 (55% in Q1FY27), sold in 100+ countries. It is Suzuki's global sourcing hub.
The clearest structural win of the last five years.
Helps everyone, but Maruti's entry-level buyers are more sensitive to interest rates. The Oct-2026 rate hike is a headwind.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the tailwinds of FY26-28 (GST cut, CNG, exports, first-time buyers) fit Maruti's strengths unusually well. They fit far better than the SUV-led cycle of FY19-25. That is the cyclical case for owning the stock now. The structural question is EVs, where Maruti is a follower.

sections.title: Star products, and where growth really comes from

blocks.p: Six of India's ten best-selling cars in FY26 were Marutis, led by the Dzire (#1, 2.29 lakh units). The volume drivers are the Dzire, Ertiga, Swift, WagonR and Baleno. The profit drivers are the SUVs sold through Nexa showrooms (Fronx, Grand Vitara and now Victoris) and the Ertiga/XL6 MPVs (multi-purpose vehicles). Note what is missing from the top of the list: **no Maruti SUV leads its segment.** Brezza and Fronx sit behind the Tata Punch and Nexon in SUVs under 4m. In mid-size SUVs, the Grand Vitara is outsold by its own Toyota-badged twin, the Hyryder.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the H1FY27 growth is real. But half of it comes from small cars, revived by a one-time tax cut, in a hatchback segment that is shrinking over time. SUVs are ≈68% of the market and earn most of its profit. There, Maruti's share is ~20%, half its overall share, and it is falling in the under-4m class it once led. Maruti leads in hatchbacks, sedans and MPVs. In the segment that matters most, it is just one of five players.

sections.title: Pipeline: many launches, but delays and a smaller EV plan

blocks.p: Management targets ~28 models by FY31 (from 17) and a return to 50% market share. Two things make us more cautious. (1) In its Feb-2025 mid-term plan, Suzuki **cut its India BEV (battery electric vehicle) plan from 6 to 4 models by FY30, and its FY30 India volume outlook to 2.54mn units** (from 3mn). (2) The most important launches (the in-house Fronx strong hybrid and the 3-row Grand Vitara) are one to two quarters later than earlier reports said. Most of the launch dates below come from press reports, not the company.

blocks.callout: **What has to go right:** for market share to rise well above 42%, two of Maruti's next five SUV launches must become top-3 sellers in their segments. Its record is mixed. Brezza, Fronx and Victoris worked; Jimny and Invicto did not; and Grand Vitara is losing to its Toyota twin. Our base case assumes no share gain after FY27. The 3-row SUV (against the XUV700 and Safari) is the launch to watch. It is Maruti's first entry into India's most profitable type of SUV.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: strong in reach, resale and CNG; not in cost or product

blocks.p: We test every claimed advantage against hard numbers. Our conclusion: Maruti's moat (lasting competitive advantage) is **distribution and trust**. It has 4,601 outlets and 5,926 service points (roughly 3x Hyundai or Tata), the best resale values in its segments, and ~70% of India's factory-fitted CNG market. This moat protects volumes in entry cars, sedans and MPVs, and generates cash through good and bad years. What it no longer has is a **cost or margin advantage**. Its Q1FY27 EBIT margin of 5.1% was below M&M's auto PBIT of 7.1% and Hyundai's EBITDA margin of ~9.3%. And it never had a product or technology lead in SUVs and EVs.

verdicts: Q1FY27 EBITDA margin: Maruti 8.6% (EBIT 5.1%) vs Hyundai Motor India ~9.25% vs Tata PV domestic 4.3% vs M&M standalone auto PBIT 7.1% (8.3% ex-eSUV contract mfg). Maruti's EBIT margin is BELOW M&M's auto PBIT and its EBITDA below Hyundai's. Scale has not given Maruti superior margins; the cost edge (localisation, scale) is…

Maruti 4,601 sales outlets (751 Nexa) and 5,926 service touchpoints (FY26) vs Hyundai 1,500+ outlets / 1,675 service touchpoints (May-2026) vs Tata PV 1,669 outlets / 1,211 service touchpoints (FY26; targeting 3,200/3,000+ by FY31). ~3x the nearest rival; 52% of FY26 sales non-urban; first-time buyers 54% in Q1FY27. M&M…

Autocar India-Spinny Used Car Study 2026 (transactions Jan-Aug 2025, 9 cities): Maruti best residual in MPVs (Ertiga), compact sedans (Dzire), premium hatch (Baleno, tied with Glanza), budget hatch (S-Presso). But NOT in SUVs: Tata Punch leads sub-compact SUVs, Kia Seltos mid-SUVs, M&M XUV700 executive SUVs; Hyundai Grand i10…

Maruti ~4% of India EV sales H1 CY2026 (6,404 e Vitara; #4) vs Tata 39%, M&M 23%, JSW MG 21%. Domestic e Vitara allocation reportedly only 2,000-2,500/month with most output exported. Suzuki cut India BEV plan from 6 to 4 models by FY30. EV penetration hit 7.6% of PV retail in Aug-2026.

Maruti ~70% of factory-fitted CNG market; CNG ~40% of Maruti volume (Q1FY27), management targeting >9 lakh CNG units in FY27. Alt-fuels (CNG+hybrid+EV) overtook petrol in Aug-2026 (CNG 25% of PV retail). Strong hybrids so far rely on Toyota tech; in-house series hybrid (Fronx) has slipped from Q2FY27 to ~2027.

Improving at the top (new Dzire: India's first 5-star BNCAP sedan, Jun-2025; Victoris 5-star BNCAP 31.66/32 AOP), but legacy volume models lag: Wagon R scored 1-star adult / 0-star child in Global NCAP 2023 (19.69/34; driver chest 'weak'). Tata and M&M have built brand around 5-star ratings across lineups (Altroz, Harrier, XEV…

Small cars: strong post-GST 2.0 (190k pending orders at FY26-end, ~130k small cars; network stock 3-4 days in Q3FY26). But in Q1FY27 Maruti could only take ~50bps price hikes (Jun + Aug) against ~300bps commodity hit - EBITDA fell 400bps YoY. SUVs: Oct-2026 Nexa discounts up to ~Rs1.36 lakh on Grand Vitara, Rs95k Invicto,…

Maruti is ~49% of India PV exports in FY26 (~55% in Q1FY27); 447,774 export units FY26 (+35%); Japan supplied from India (Fronx/Jimny/e Vitara). Exports cushion domestic cyclicality, though Q2FY27 exports fell 2% YoY.

UVs ~68% of PV market; Maruti SUV share ~19.6% (FY26) vs ~79% in hatches. Sub-4m SUV share fell from ~30% (May-23) to ~26% (Q2 CY26) as Tata Punch/Nexon took #1/#2; Grand Vitara outsold by its Toyota twin Hyryder (78,140 vs 61,687 Jan-Sep 2026); Invicto 1,635 units in H1FY27 vs Innova ~8-10k/month.

blocks.h: What critics say, and whether we agree

exhibit.title: The bear points we take seriously
head: Criticism
Source
Our view
rows: Maruti's FY26 domestic share slipped to a 13-year low as buyers shifted to SUVs; M&M (14.2%) became No.2 and Tata ~13%, while Maruti still claims a 50% share target by FY31.
Agree. The 13-year low in market share in FY26 is the clearest evidence that the old moat has narrowed.
The H1FY27 share recovery (to ~41%) is driven by the GST 2.0 small-car tax cut - a one-time policy tailwind in a shrinking hatch segment, not a structural win in SUVs.
Analyst synthesis from AngelOne H1FY27 share…
Partly agree. The GST cut is one-off. But it restarts first-time buying, and those buyers later upgrade within the Maruti network.
Wagon R - a top-5 car - got 1 star (adult) and 0 stars (child) in Global NCAP's 2023 test, with 'weak' driver chest protection.
Agree; this is a real brand risk. Newer models are safer (Dzire and Victoris have 5-star Bharat NCAP crash ratings), but older high-volume models lag.
Late and reluctant EV entrant: rivals Tata, JSW MG and M&M already locked in early adopters; Tata holds >40% EV share.
Agree. EVs are Maruti's biggest strategic gap. CNG and hybrids buy time but are not a substitute.
Cut near-term e Vitara production by about two-thirds (8,200 vs 26,500 planned for Apr-Sep 2025) due to Chinese rare-earth magnet curbs - exposes supply-chain dependence.
Agree. Reliance on China for magnets is a risk across the sector, and Maruti has not solved it.
Suzuki scaled back its India EV ambitions to 4 BEVs by FY30 (from 6) and cut its long-term India volume outlook to 2.54mn units by FY30 from 3mn.
Agree. A lower FY30 Suzuki outlook caps the long-term volume story.
Q1FY27 operating margin collapsed to 5.1% EBIT (from 8.8% in Q4FY26) on aluminium/commodity costs and a supplier-settlement change; stock ~-22% from end-July to 52-week low by 22-Oct-2026.
Agree on the facts, but we think ~60% of the hit will reverse (see the margins chapter).
Toyota alliance cannibalises: the Toyota-made Hyryder outsells Maruti's own Grand Vitara (13.0% vs 10.3% mid-SUV share Jan-Sep 2026) and Maruti's Invicto is a non-starter next to Innova Hycross.
Data from Autopunditz; Outlook Business noted…
Agree. The Toyota alliance gives Maruti extra volume (cars it supplies to Toyota), but it also strengthens a competitor in its own segments.
exhibit.source: Media and analyst sources as cited, GAM Research

blocks.callout: **Bottom line on the moat:** Maruti is a high-reach, high-trust volume business. It resembles Toyota in Japan (a long-standing leader with ~30% share) more than a premium compounder. That earns a steady 10-12% EBITDA margin and strong cash flow, but not monopoly-level profits. **Today it has no competitive advantage in SUVs, EVs or cost per car**, and investors should not pay for one.

sections.title: Per-car economics: what drove the margin low

blocks.p: Revenue per vehicle has risen almost every year since FY15 (₹3.8 lakh → ₹7.2 lakh). Yet EBITDA (operating profit) per vehicle rose only ~40% over the same period (₹63k in FY16 → ₹89k in FY26). So each rupee of revenue now earns less. The gap is cost. Raw materials went from 67% of sales (FY16) to 72% (FY26) and 77% (Q1FY27). Precious metals, steel and aluminium became costlier, and the mix shifted back to small cars after GST 2.0.

pair.title: EBITDA per car up ~40% since FY16, but price per car up ~80%
Raw-material cost is the biggest swing factor

blocks.h: The per-car cost lines that matter

blocks.p: Four cost lines explain most of the per-car economics. **Discounts** (deducted from revenue) rose from ~₹19.6k per car in FY18 to ~₹29.8k in FY25 as competition grew. They eased to ~₹26.6k in FY26. **Royalty** paid to Suzuki fell from 5.8% of sales (FY16) to 3.1% (FY26). This is a real gain for minority shareholders. (Before the SMG merger, part of the royalty sat inside purchase costs, so the FY18-24 figures understate it.) **Employee cost per car** has tripled since FY15 (₹12k → ₹37k), growing faster than revenue per car. **Plant utilisation** is back near 98% (FY26). That is why the two new plants matter for FY27 volumes. But they also add fixed costs before they fill up.

Royalty to Suzuki: 5.8% → 3.1% of sales

blocks.p: Management's margin bridge for Q1FY27 shows that commodities did almost all the damage. Standalone EBITDA margin fell to 8.6%, from 12.3% in Q4FY26. Importantly, ~110bp of the commodity hit came from a temporary change in how supplier price adjustments are settled (moved from a quarterly to a monthly lag). That part reverses. Price hikes (~50bp in June, and a second round from August) were not yet in the quarter's numbers.

pair.title: Our forecast: margins recover, but not to FY24-25 levels

blocks.callout: **Why we do not model a 13% margin again:** (1) GST-led demand favours small cars, which earn roughly half the per-unit margin of SUVs. (2) Two new 250k plants plus Khoraj add depreciation and start-up costs before they are fully used. (3) EVs launch at thin or negative margins. (4) With six players in SUVs, discounts stay structurally higher. Every 100bp of EBITDA margin is ~₹2,400 cr of EBITDA, roughly 10% of FY28E EPS.

Depreciation is rising with the new plants

sections.title: Exports are a real second engine; in EVs Maruti is catching up

blocks.p: Exports are the clearest structural improvement in Maruti's business in a decade. Volumes rose from ~96k units in FY21 to {{kpi.exports.11|num}} in FY26. That is 18.5% of Maruti's total volume and ~49% of all passenger vehicles India exports (55% in Q1FY27). Three things changed. First, Suzuki moved global sourcing of small cars and the Jimny and Fronx to India. Second, India's rupee cost base became competitive in Africa, Latin America and the Middle East. Third, from Aug-2025 India became the global production base for Suzuki's first EV, the e-Vitara, which ships to Europe and Japan.

pair.title: Exports as a share of Maruti volume: 8% → 18% in five years
Maruti's share of India's PV exports
pair.source: SIAM, company, GAM Research (FY25 not disclosed on a comparable basis)

blocks.p: **A caveat:** export growth stalled in Jul-Aug 2026 (−5% YoY). The West Asia conflict hurt freight and key Middle-East and African markets. Management declined to give FY27 export guidance ("help me predict the war"). Maruti earns more per car on exports than at home, so this affects mix as well as volume. We model flat to modest export growth in FY27-28.

blocks.h: EVs: late, export-first, and not yet a factor at home

blocks.p: EVs reached ~7.6% of India's retail car sales in Aug-2026. Tata leads (~39% of EVs), followed by M&M (~24%) and JSW MG (~20%). Maruti's e-Vitara launched in Aug-2025 for export and in Feb-2026 in India. Only ~2,000-2,500 a month go to the domestic market, giving Maruti ~4% of India's EV market (#4). In Feb-2025 Suzuki cut its India BEV (battery electric vehicle) plan from 6 to 4 models by FY30. So Maruti is entering a segment where three rivals have a 4-5 year head start in product, charging partnerships and brand. In our base case Maruti wins a below-fair share of EVs (~15-20%). We assume the shift to EVs stays gradual through FY30, and that Maruti's CNG and hybrid range protects it in the meantime.

sections.title: A very strong balance sheet that holds back returns

blocks.p: Maruti has had almost no debt for a decade. Cash and investments of ₹{{fin.treasury.11|num}} cr at FY26 equal ~73% of net worth and ~23% of market value. This matters to shareholders in two ways. (1) The cash earns only ~6-7% before tax. So headline ROE (return on equity: profit ÷ shareholders' funds) of {{fin.roe.11|pct}} in FY26 badly understates the business. Return on operating capital (the return on the money actually used in the car business, excluding cash) is above 50%. (2) Other income is a large and volatile part of profit. It fell 12% in FY26 because of mark-to-market (MTM) losses, i.e. falls in the market value of its bonds.

pair.title: Headline ROE vs the car business's own return
Where 12 years of operating cash went

blocks.p: Capital allocation has been conservative, not value-destroying. There have been no large acquisitions and no diversification. Maruti pays out 30-35% of profit as dividends and sizes capex to demand. The SMG share swap (2023) was the one disputed decision. Minority shareholders questioned whether it was fair to issue 1.23 crore shares to Suzuki for a plant Suzuki had funded. In our view it was roughly value-neutral. The real criticism is the cost of idle cash. A cash-heavy balance sheet with no buybacks has kept ROE in the teens.

sections.title: Who owns the stock: foreign investors sold, LIC bought

blocks.p: Suzuki Motor Corp owns {{SH.rows.Promoters.11|pct}} and has been quietly buying (+1.4mn shares since Dec-25). This signals the parent's own view on value. The shareholder register explains why the valuation fell. **FIIs (foreign institutional investors) cut their stake from 20.6% (Dec-23) to 12.4% (Sep-26)**. There were 86 fewer foreign holders in the last quarter alone. The main buyer has been **LIC (4.3% → 5.85% in nine months)**, along with NPS (the National Pension System). Mutual funds were net sellers in the Sep-26 quarter (ICICI Pru, Kotak and UTI down; HDFC up). Nippon and PPFAS fell below the 1% level at which holdings must be disclosed. Retail shareholders rose by ~65,000 to 4.3 lakh, buying the fall.

sections.title: Governance and the Suzuki relationship: mostly clean, three flags

blocks.p: Maruti is a Suzuki subsidiary. It has a Japanese MD & CEO (Hisashi Takeuchi), a non-executive Indian chairman (R.C. Bhargava, chairman for over two decades) and 7 Japanese nationals on a 12-member board. Related-party transactions (payments between Maruti and Suzuki) are large, but they have become cheaper for minority shareholders. **Royalty fell from ~4.8% to ~3.1% of sales**, as new models moved to a lower royalty paid in rupees. Minority votes against Suzuki-related resolutions have been small (1.8-3.2% against the 2023 SMG deal). The exception was the 2015 vote on Gujarat contract manufacturing (10.3% against).

The BUY therefore does not depend on any one model: Maruti is cheap on its own history, on cash flows and on operating profit.

blocks.p: We value Maruti with a 15-year DCF (discounted cash flow: today's value of the cash the business will generate). We use free cash flow to the firm (FCFF), excluding treasury income, and add net cash separately. Cost of equity (the return shareholders require) is {{dcf.ke|pct}}. That is a 6.6% risk-free rate plus 0.85 beta (sensitivity to the market) × a 6% equity risk premium (ERP). Maruti has no debt, so its WACC (weighted average cost of capital) equals the cost of equity. Nominal growth slows from ~10% to 8.5% by FY41E, and EBITDA margin settles at 12.5%. After that we assume 5.5% terminal growth (the long-run growth rate forever). Terminal value is {{dcf.tvShare|pct0}} of enterprise value.

We think a 25-28x forward P/E (price ÷ next year's earnings) is fair for an Indian volume leader with net cash and ~10% earnings growth.

sections.title: Our honest summary: what you own, and how to size it

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's most trusted volume car maker, with the widest reach (4,601 outlets, six of the top-10 models, best resale values). It has ~₹{{fin.treasury.11|num}} cr of net cash and pays out 30%+ of profit as dividends. It has a lasting export business and the most direct exposure to GST 2.0 and first-time car buyers. And it trades at {{V.pe.current|x}} trailing earnings, the cheapest in a decade.

**What you are not buying:** a monopoly, a technology leader or a premium brand that compounds for decades. Maruti lost ~10 points of market share in the SUV decade and has no lead in EVs. Its margins depend more on commodity prices and the yen than on its own decisions. Earnings have been flat for two years and analysts are still cutting forecasts. It is no longer the most profitable mass-market OEM (car maker). And an unexplained auditor resignation (2025) is a governance question worth asking.

blocks.h: How we would use it in a portfolio

bullets: **Role:** a value and cash-flow holding within consumer discretionary. It is a cyclical recovery play with balance-sheet support, not a long-term compounder.
**Expected return:** base-case target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}) plus ~1.3% dividend yield. Bear case: {{scen.bear.tp|inr}} ({{scen.bear.upside|chg}}).
**Sizing:** the upside outweighs the downside, but the stock is not risk-free. Earnings momentum is RED, so we would build the position in stages around the Q2/Q3FY27 results rather than all at once.
**What would make us buy more:** EBITDA margin back above 10.5% in Q2/Q3FY27; FII (foreign institutional investor) holding starting to rise; a successful 3-row SUV launch.
**What would make us sell:** margins stuck below 9.5% through FY27; domestic share back below 39%; evidence that GST demand was a one-off pull-forward.

sections.title: Glossary

blocks.p: Plain-English definitions of the technical terms used in this report.

exhibit.title: Glossary of terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: operating profit before non-cash charges. The margin is EBITDA as a % of sales.
Operating profit after depreciation (EBIT), or profit before interest and tax (PBIT). Some companies report one, some the other.
Profit after tax (net profit) and profit before tax.
Earnings per share: net profit divided by the number of shares.
Price-to-earnings ratio: share price divided by EPS. "Trailing" uses the last 12 months of earnings.
Enterprise value (market value plus debt, minus cash) divided by EBITDA. It compares companies regardless of how much cash or debt they hold.
Discounted cash flow: valuing a company on the cash it will generate in future, converted into today's money.
Free cash flow: operating cash flow minus capex. FCFF (free cash flow to the firm) is the cash available to all investors before financing.
The annual return shareholders require (cost of equity). WACC (weighted average cost of capital) blends this with the cost of debt; for a debt-free company like Maruti they are the same.
Beta measures how much a stock moves with the market. The equity risk premium is the extra return investors demand for owning shares instead of government bonds.
The growth rate assumed for every year after the forecast period, and the value of all those later cash flows.
Return on equity: net profit as a % of shareholders' funds.
Return earned on the money used in the car business itself, excluding surplus cash and investments.
When sales rise, fixed costs are spread over more units and margins rise faster; when sales fall, the reverse happens.
100bp = 1 percentage point (ppt). A margin moving from 10.0% to 11.5% is a 150bp rise.
Valuing investments at today's market price. Gains or losses flow through other income even if nothing is sold.
A 2nd-percentile valuation is cheaper than 98% of past readings. Standard deviation measures how far a value usually swings from its average.
Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly growth that turns a starting value into an ending value.
Original equipment manufacturer: here, a car maker such as Maruti, Hyundai, Tata or M&M.
Passenger vehicles (cars, utility vehicles and vans). Utility vehicles (UVs) are mostly SUVs, sport utility vehicles.
Wholesale is cars dispatched from the factory to dealers. Retail is cars sold by dealers to customers. A gap means dealer stock is building or falling.
Compressed natural gas: a cheaper fuel than petrol; Maruti sells factory-fitted CNG cars.
Battery electric vehicle (runs only on a battery) and hybrid electric vehicle (combines a petrol engine with a battery and electric motor). EV covers electric cars in general.
Bharat Stage VI: India's emission norms, introduced in April 2020, which raised the cost of cars, especially diesel cars.
Corporate Average Fuel Efficiency norms, phase III: limits on the average fuel use and emissions across a car maker's range.
Platinum-group metals (platinum, palladium, rhodium) used in catalytic converters that clean exhaust gases.
The September 2025 GST revision, which cut the tax on small cars from 28% plus cess to 18%.
Suzuki Motor Gujarat, the plant Maruti bought from Suzuki in 2023. Because both are controlled by Suzuki, past figures were restated as if the two had always been combined.
Fees Maruti pays Suzuki for technology and brand. Related-party transactions are dealings with the parent or group companies, disclosed in the annual report.
Possible future payments, such as disputed tax claims, that depend on the outcome of a case.
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal: the body that hears appeals in tax disputes.
Extended producer responsibility: rules that make manufacturers responsible for recycling or disposing of products at end of life.
Foreign institutional (or portfolio) investors and domestic institutional investors such as mutual funds and insurers.
The average forecast of analysts who cover the stock.

statementNotes.ebitda@FY20: BS-VI transition and exit from diesel. Domestic volumes −16% with record discounts; fixed costs spread over fewer cars (negative operating leverage).

statementNotes.ebitda@FY23: Operating recovery plus an accounting effect. FY23 is restated for the SMG acquisition as if the two firms had always been combined (common-control pooling). This moves SMG's plant depreciation out of material cost, adding roughly 170bp to EBITDA margin vs FY22.
statementNotes.ebitda@FY24: More SUVs, lower discounts (₹14.5k per vehicle in Q4 vs ₹23k) and cheaper precious metals.
statementNotes.ebitda@FY26: EBITDA rose only 6.5% while revenue rose 20%. Reasons: more small cars after GST 2.0, model price cuts (−70bp), commodities and a one-off labour-code provision (Q3).
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY16: Peak-margin year: falling commodity prices, a favourable yen and more premium Baleno/Brezza sales.
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY19: Higher commodity prices (steel, PGMs), a stronger yen and higher discounts as demand slowed in H2.
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY20: BS-VI cost, diesel exit and volume collapse.
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY22: Record-low margin. The chip shortage idled plants while steel and PGM prices peaked. Price hikes lagged costs.
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY23: Volume recovery and commodity relief, plus ~170bp from the SMG restatement (see EBITDA note).
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY24: Best year since FY18: SUV mix, cost reduction and lower discounts.
statementNotes.ebitdaMargin@FY26: GST demand led by small cars, price cuts, commodities and Kharkhoda start-up costs.
statementNotes.materialPct@FY16: Falling commodity prices, more local sourcing and the yen.
statementNotes.materialPct@FY22: Steel, aluminium and PGMs at record highs.
statementNotes.materialPct@FY23: Commodities eased. The SMG restatement also moved depreciation out of material cost.
statementNotes.materialPct@FY24: Cheaper PGMs, cost cutting and SUV pricing.
statementNotes.materialPct@FY26: GST pass-through and model price cuts lowered revenue per car while commodity costs rose.
statementNotes.materialPct@FY17: Commodities turned up (steel) and the yen strengthened after the FY16 lows.
statementNotes.otherIncome@FY20: Larger treasury and gains as yields fell after RBI rate cuts.
statementNotes.otherIncome@FY23: Higher yields lifted interest income on a larger investment book.
statementNotes.receivables@FY19: Dealer receivables rose as demand slowed in H2FY19 (still only ~10 days of sales).
statementNotes.receivables@FY22: Export receivables rose with exports more than doubling.
statementNotes.receivables@FY23: Exports and higher volumes; receivables remain ~10 days of sales.
statementNotes.payables@FY16: Higher production. Suppliers typically give ~55-70 days of credit.
statementNotes.payables@FY21: Production surge in H2FY21 after the lockdown.
statementNotes.payables@FY23: Volumes +19% and the SMG restatement (Gujarat supplier payables consolidated).
statementNotes.capex@FY22: Resumption of deferred capex and product development after COVID.
statementNotes.otherIncome@FY16: Growing treasury: cash not spent on the Gujarat plant (funded by Suzuki) was invested.
statementNotes.otherIncome@FY17: Larger treasury plus mark-to-market gains as yields fell.
statementNotes.otherIncome@FY22: Mark-to-market losses on debt funds as bond yields rose.
statementNotes.otherIncome@FY24: Larger investment book and MTM gains as yields eased.
statementNotes.dep@FY23: SMG restatement: Gujarat plant depreciation now consolidated.
statementNotes.pat@FY23: Recovery from the FY22 trough on volume, pricing and commodity relief.
statementNotes.pat@FY26: Profit flat (+1%) despite +20% revenue: lower margins, depreciation +20% and an MTM loss on treasury (~₹750 cr in Q4).
statementNotes.equityShares@FY24: 1.23 crore new shares issued to Suzuki for 100% of SMG (~4% dilution).
statementNotes.capex@FY23: Work starts on the new Kharkhoda plant; restated to include SMG capex.
statementNotes.cfo@FY19: Working capital: payables fell as production slowed in H2.
statementNotes.cfo@FY20: Volume slump and BS-VI inventory transition.
statementNotes.cfo@FY21: Payables jumped as production surged in H2 after lockdown.
statementNotes.cfo@FY22: Lower supplier payables, extra inventory during the chip shortage, and higher taxes.
statementNotes.receivables@FY25: Export growth (export receivables carry longer terms).
statementNotes.inventoryDays@FY26: Inventory days rose to 31 from 23, as stock was built for exports and the new plant. This is the first reversal of a decade-long improvement.
statementNotes.investments@FY16: Treasury build after Suzuki took on Gujarat plant capex.
statementNotes.sales@Q3FY26: First full quarter of GST 2.0: domestic +22%, record retail ~684k.
statementNotes.ebitda@Q1FY25: Compared against a weak Q1FY24 (one-off costs); cheaper commodities.
statementNotes.ebitda@Q4FY26: Record volumes spread fixed costs (operating leverage); no repeat of the labour-code one-off.
statementNotes.opm@Q2FY24: Record revenue per car (+15% YoY on more UVs) and cheaper precious metals.
statementNotes.opm@Q1FY27: Commodities ~300bp (incl. ~110bp from settlement timing), FX, inventory and employee costs. See the margin bridge.
statementNotes.materialPct@Q1FY25: Reversal of a Q4 one-off and softer commodities.
statementNotes.materialPct@Q3FY26: GST price pass-through, model price cuts and commodities.
statementNotes.materialPct@Q1FY27: West Asia commodity shock (aluminium, plastics, gas) and supplier settlement timing.
statementNotes.otherIncome@Q4FY26: ~₹750 cr MTM loss as bond yields rose (West Asia).
statementNotes.otherIncome@Q1FY27: MTM reversal and a larger treasury.
statementNotes.pat@Q2FY25: One-time ~₹837 cr deferred-tax charge after the tax benefit on debt funds (indexation) was removed.
statementNotes.pat@Q1FY27: PAT −9% despite +36% revenue: the margin low point.
